options: Synarthroses are fibrous and immobile joints
Amphiarthroses are fibrous and immobile joints
Diarthroses are synovial and mobile joints
Amphiarthroses are cartilaginous and semi-mobile joints
The articular system is studied by myology
questions.explanation: By structure/mobility: synarthroses = fibrous/immobile, amphiarthroses = cartilaginous/semi-mobile, diarthroses = synovial/mobile. The articular system is studied by arthrology.

options: Include the gomphosis uniting a tooth to its socket
Have no articular cartilage
Include the synfibroses of the skull and face
Are semi-mobile joints
Include the pubic symphysis
questions.explanation: Synarthroses are immobile fibrous joints without articular cartilage (synfibroses, syndesmoses, gomphosis). The pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis (semi-mobile).

questions.stem: The interosseous membrane between the two bones of the forearm is an example of:
options: A synfibrosis
A syndesmosis
A symphysis
A synchondrosis
A gomphosis
questions.explanation: Syndesmoses unite bony surfaces distant from each other by connective tissue: interosseous membrane of forearm/leg, ligamenta flava between vertebrae.

options: Are permanent fibrous joints of the skull
Are located between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of long bones
Are synovial joints
Correspond to the growth plate responsible for longitudinal growth
Are temporary joints during growth
questions.explanation: Synchondroses (amphiarthroses) are temporary: the growth (conjugation) plate between epiphysis and diaphysis. Trauma can cause epiphyseal detachment.

options: Are reinforced by peripheral ligaments
Are exemplified by the pubic symphysis
Have a synovial membrane
Unite bony surfaces by a mixed fibrous and fibrocartilaginous structure
Are semi-mobile joints
questions.explanation: Symphyses are amphiarthroses with reduced mobility; a synovial membrane characterizes diarthroses.

options: Being a minority of the limb joints
Epiphyseal articular surfaces covered with hyaline cartilage
An articular cavity
An articular gap of a few centimetres
A synovial membrane
questions.explanation: The articular gap is only a few millimetres, and synovial joints make up the majority of limb joints.

options: Has a thickness inversely proportional to the pressure it supports
Has the same thickness in all joints
Its degeneration is responsible for arthrosis (osteoarthritis)
Is richly vascularized
Is smooth and bluish-white
questions.explanation: Thickness varies with the pressure supported, so it is not constant between joints. Also false: "Has a thickness inversely proportional to the pressure it supports"; "Is richly vascularized".

options: The synovial membrane is poorly vascularized and not innervated
It is a fibrous sleeve inserting around the articular surfaces
Its external part is the fibrous membrane
The synovial membrane lines the external face of the capsule
Its internal part is the synovial membrane
questions.explanation: The synovial membrane lines the inner face of the capsule and is richly vascularized and innervated.

options: Facilitates the gliding of the articular surfaces
Is secreted by the fibrous membrane
Is secreted by the synovial membrane
Plays no role in the nutrition of the articular surfaces
Is opaque and watery
questions.explanation: Synovia is produced by the synovial membrane, not the fibrous membrane. Also false: "Is opaque and watery"; "Plays no role in the nutrition of the articular surfaces".

questions.stem: After a knee injury, a patient has blood in the joint cavity. This is called:
options: Hydarthrosis
Luxation
Hemarthrosis
Bursitis
Arthrosis
questions.explanation: Hemarthrosis = blood effusion in a joint after trauma. Hydarthrosis = effusion/hypersecretion of synovial fluid.

questions.stem: About the stabilizers of a synovial joint:
options: Tendons of periarticular muscles are the means of active stabilization
Ligaments are fibrous bands uniting the constituent parts of the joint
Ligaments are the means of passive stabilization
Tendons of periarticular muscles are passive stabilizers
Ligaments are the means of active stabilization
questions.explanation: Ligaments = passive stabilization; periarticular muscle tendons = active stabilization.

questions.stem: The means of adaptation of synovial joints:
options: Are of three types: labrum, meniscus and disc
Are interposed between the capsule and the synovial membrane
Are fibrocartilaginous structures
Are richly vascularized, so their tears heal well
Exist in all joints, whatever their congruence
questions.explanation: Fibrocartilages are devoid of vessels and nerves; this lack of vascularization prevents healing of tears. Also false: "Exist in all joints, whatever their congruence"; "Are interposed between the capsule and the synovial membrane".

questions.stem: Match the means of adaptation with its example:
options: Meniscus: the coxofemoral joint
Labrum: the scapulohumeral and coxofemoral joints
Labrum: the intervertebral disc
Meniscus: the knee and the acromioclavicular joint
Disc: the intervertebral disc and the sternoclavicular joint
questions.explanation: Menisci: knee (medial and lateral), acromioclavicular. Labrum: shoulder and hip. Disc: intervertebral, sternoclavicular.

options: Is a fibrocartilaginous ring
Increases the depth and surface area of the articular zone
Its main role is shock absorption of pressure and traction
Inserts on the periphery of the bony articular zone
Is found in the knee
questions.explanation: Shock absorption and distribution of pressure/traction is the role of discs; the knee has menisci.

questions.stem: A footballer has a torn meniscal fragment causing symptoms. Why must it usually be removed?
options: Because the meniscus heals spontaneously in a few days
Because fibrocartilage is devoid of vessels, so the tear cannot heal
Because the meniscus is richly innervated and always painful
Because the meniscus is made of hyaline cartilage
Because the meniscus is an active stabilizer
questions.explanation: The absence of vascularization prevents healing of a fibrocartilaginous tear, so a symptomatic torn fragment must be removed (e.g. by arthroscopy).

questions.stem: Match the type of synovial joint with its example:
options: Spheroid (enarthrosis): scapulohumeral and coxofemoral joints
Trochoid (pivot): humero-ulnar joint
Sellar (saddle): carpometacarpal joint of the thumb
Plane (arthrodia): proximal radio-ulnar joint
Ellipsoid (condylar): radiocarpal joint
questions.explanation: The humero-ulnar joint is trochlear (ginglymus); radio-ulnar joints are trochoid; the acromioclavicular joint is plane.

questions.stem: How many axes of mobility does each joint type have?
options: Spheroid: three axes
Sellar: two axes
Ellipsoid: three axes
Trochlear: two axes
Ellipsoid: one axis
questions.explanation: Spheroid 3 axes (great mobility), ellipsoid and sellar 2 axes, trochlear (hinge) 1 axis. Also false: "Ellipsoid: one axis"; "Trochlear: two axes".

options: Unites two inverted spherical surfaces
Unites surfaces convex in one direction and concave in the other
Is also called a joint by reciprocal reception
Has two axes of mobility
Unites two flat surfaces
questions.explanation: Flat surfaces = plane joint (arthrodia); inverted spheres = spheroid joint.

options: Extension "opens" the joint
Flexion "closes" the joint around a transverse axis
Lateral rotation moves the anterior face of the segment outward
Medial rotation moves the anterior face of the segment outward
Abduction is performed around a vertical axis
questions.explanation: Abduction/adduction occur around a sagittal axis; medial rotation moves the anterior face inward.

questions.stem: About exploration and pathology of joints:
options: Clinical examination is unilateral and only passive
A luxation (dislocation) is a loss of contact between two articular surfaces
Ultrasound and especially MRI show the articular cartilage and fibrocartilages
Arthrosis is an infectious arthritis
A sprain is a loss of contact between two articular surfaces
questions.explanation: Arthrosis is degenerative; arthritis is infectious or inflammatory. Also false: "Clinical examination is unilateral and only passive"; "A sprain is a loss of contact between two articular surfaces".

options: Is a direct endoscopy of the joint cavities
Is an injection of contrast medium into the joint
Is the simplest and most practised joint examination
Can be used to remove torn meniscal fragments
Visualizes intra-articular structures
questions.explanation: Contrast injection is arthrography; the simplest and most practised examination is standard radiography.
